subtopic_detail: shallow ulcer above the inner ankle with brown staining that improves when the leg is raised
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 69-year-old retired nurse with an ulcer on her left lower leg that has been present for four months. It aches by the end of the day and the ache eases when she puts her feet up on the lounge in the evening.

She stood for long shifts for thirty years and has varicose veins on both legs. She has hypertension and a body mass index of 31 kg per square metre, and she has never smoked and has no diabetes. On examination there is a shallow ulcer 4 cm across with a sloping edge and a granulating base just above the medial malleolus. The surrounding skin is brown stained with pitting oedema and firm inelastic skin over the lower third of the calf. The foot is warm and pink with normal capillary refill, and dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are both palpable. Monofilament sensation is intact at all sites. The ankle brachial pressure index is 1.0 on the affected side.

data_table.Examination: Shallow 4 cm ulcer with sloping edge and granulating base above the medial malleolus, haemosiderin staining, pitting oedema, lipodermatosclerosis
data_table.Vascular: Warm pink foot, normal capillary refill, palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, ankle brachial pressure index 1.0
data_table.Neurological: Monofilament sensation intact at all tested sites, no deformity or callus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply a hydrocolloid dressing with weekly review and referral for vascular surgical assessment
options.rationale: Venous duplex assessment with a view to superficial venous intervention is worthwhile and reduces recurrence, so referral belongs in the plan. A dressing without compression does not heal a venous ulcer, and omitting compression is the single commonest reason these ulcers persist for years. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Arrange urgent arterial duplex imaging and refer to vascular surgery for consideration of bypass
options.rationale: This is the pathway for an arterial ulcer, the near pair, which sits over the toes, heel or lateral malleolus with a punched out edge, a pale base, absent pulses and an ankle brachial index below 0.8. Palpable pulses and an index of 1.0 exclude significant arterial disease. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Take a wound swab for culture and commence oral cefalexin pending the microbiology result
options.rationale: All chronic ulcers are colonised, so a positive swab reflects surface flora rather than infection and prompts unnecessary antibiotics. Treatment is reserved for clinical infection with spreading erythema, increasing pain, purulence or systemic features, none of which is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply graduated multilayer compression bandaging with a simple non adherent wound dressing
options.rationale: A shallow sloping edged ulcer in the gaiter area with haemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis is venous, and an ankle brachial pressure index of 1.0 confirms that compression is safe. Graduated compression is the intervention that heals venous ulcers, and the dressing choice itself makes little difference. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Refer to a podiatrist for pressure offloading footwear and daily inspection of both feet
options.rationale: Offloading is the cornerstone of neuropathic ulcer management, which occurs at pressure points on the plantar surface in a patient with sensory loss. Intact monofilament sensation and an ulcer in the gaiter area rather than under the foot point away from that mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Wound care)

explanation.summary: Venous leg ulceration results from sustained ambulatory venous hypertension, and around 70 per cent of leg ulcers in Australia are venous in origin. The characteristic picture is a shallow ulcer with a sloping irregular edge in the gaiter region, most often above the medial malleolus, surrounded by haemosiderin staining, varicose eczema and lipodermatosclerosis, with an aching leg that is relieved by elevation. Graduated multilayer compression delivering around 40 mmHg at the ankle is the treatment that heals these ulcers, and dressing selection has repeatedly been shown to matter far less than whether compression is applied. Measuring the ankle brachial pressure index before compression is mandatory, because applying compression to a limb with significant arterial disease can cause tissue necrosis; an index between 0.8 and 1.3 permits full compression, lower values require modified or no compression with vascular referral, and values above 1.3 suggest incompressible calcified vessels needing a toe pressure instead. Early endovenous ablation of superficial reflux speeds healing and reduces recurrence, and lifelong compression hosiery after healing is what prevents the ulcer coming back.
key_points: Shallow sloping edged gaiter area ulcer with haemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis.
Measure the ankle brachial pressure index before applying any compression.
Graduated multilayer compression is the intervention that heals; the dressing matters little.
Swabs reflect colonisation; treat only clinically infected ulcers with antibiotics.
Ongoing compression hosiery after healing prevents recurrence.
explanation.pearls: An ankle brachial pressure index above 1.3 does not mean excellent arterial supply but incompressible calcified vessels, most often in diabetes or chronic kidney disease, and a toe brachial index below 0.7 is what confirms arterial disease in that situation.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

subtopic_detail: thickened crumbling discolouration of several toenails in a man who wants treatment before a holiday
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 54-year-old man who is embarrassed about his toenails and wants them treated before a beach holiday. Over about three years the nails have become thickened, yellow brown and crumbly, and the first, third and fourth toenails on the right foot and the first on the left are affected.

He has no diabetes, no peripheral vascular symptoms and takes no regular medications. He plays squash twice a week and uses communal changing rooms. On examination the affected nails are thickened with subungual debris lifting the nail plate from the bed at the free edge, and the discolouration runs from the distal edge proximally. There is fine scaling in the fourth toe web spaces bilaterally. The unaffected nails are normal, there is no nail pitting, no oil drop sign and no skin plaques at the elbows, knees or scalp. Pedal pulses are palpable, the feet are warm and monofilament sensation is intact.

data_table.Examination: Four thickened yellow brown nails with distal subungual hyperkeratosis and onycholysis, fine interdigital scaling in the fourth web spaces
data_table.Negative findings: No nail pitting, no oil drop discolouration, no cutaneous psoriatic plaques, no nail fold inflammation
data_table.Vascular and neurological: Palpable pedal pulses, warm feet, intact monofilament sensation, no diabetes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send nail clippings with subungual debris for microscopy and culture before prescribing
options.rationale: Only about half of dystrophic nails are fungal, and oral terbinafine is a months long course requiring liver monitoring, so laboratory confirmation is required before treatment. Clippings taken from the proximal edge of the affected area with subungual debris give the best yield. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Refer to a dermatologist for a nail matrix biopsy to establish the underlying diagnosis
options.rationale: Nail biopsy is reserved for suspected melanoma of the nail unit or for dystrophy that remains unexplained after negative mycology. It is invasive and painful compared with a clipping that answers the question here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid under occlusion to the nail folds for eight weeks
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid is directed at nail psoriasis, the near pair, which is distinguished by pitting, an oil drop discolouration through the nail plate, and cutaneous plaques elsewhere. Distal onycholysis with subungual debris and coexisting tinea pedis points to a dermatophyte instead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Prescribe an amorolfine nail lacquer applied weekly for twelve months with regular nail filing
options.rationale: Topical lacquer is a reasonable option for superficial or distal disease affecting a small number of nails without matrix involvement, and it avoids systemic exposure. Cure rates are low for thickened nails with substantial subungual hyperkeratosis, and the diagnosis is still unconfirmed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence oral terbinafine for three months with liver function testing at baseline and six weeks
options.rationale: This is the correct regimen and the correct monitoring for confirmed dermatophyte toenail disease, so the treatment plan itself is sound. Committing him to three months of systemic therapy without mycological confirmation is what the guidance specifically advises against. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Onychomycosis accounts for roughly half of all nail dystrophy, with the remainder caused by psoriasis, trauma, lichen planus and, rarely, subungual melanoma. Dermatophytes, principally Trichophyton rubrum, cause most cases, and coexisting tinea pedis is a useful supporting clue since the nail is usually infected from the adjacent skin. Because the appearance is not reliable enough to commit a patient to months of systemic antifungal therapy with its hepatic monitoring and drug interactions, confirmation by microscopy and culture on nail clippings is recommended before treatment. Sampling technique matters: clippings should be taken as proximally as possible within the affected area together with subungual debris, since the distal nail plate often contains only non viable organisms. Oral terbinafine is first line for dermatophyte nail disease, given for six weeks for fingernails and three months for toenails, and cure is judged by the growth of healthy nail rather than by immediate appearance, which takes twelve to eighteen months for a great toenail.
key_points: Only about half of dystrophic nails are fungal, so confirm before systemic treatment.
Coexisting tinea pedis supports a dermatophyte source; pitting suggests psoriasis instead.
Sample proximally within the affected nail and include subungual debris.
Oral terbinafine runs six weeks for fingernails and three months for toenails.
A single dark longitudinal band with proximal nail fold pigment needs melanoma exclusion.
explanation.pearls: Warn the patient that the nail will not look normal at the end of treatment: a great toenail grows about 1 mm a month, so a visually acceptable result takes twelve to eighteen months after a three month course and the absence of immediate change is not treatment failure.

subtopic_detail: woman with central facial flushing and papules whose eyes are gritty with crusted lid margins
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46-year-old woman with two years of facial redness that she has treated as sensitive skin. She flushes with red wine, hot drinks and stepping into a warm room, and over the past six months small red bumps have appeared across her cheeks and nose.

She has used a topical corticosteroid cream prescribed for eczema intermittently over the past year, which helps for a few days before the redness returns worse. She also mentions that her eyes have felt gritty and dry for months and that her eyelids are crusted in the mornings. On examination there is persistent erythema with telangiectasia across the cheeks, nose and chin, with scattered papules and pustules and no comedones. The eyelid margins are thickened and erythematous with crusting at the lash bases, and the conjunctivae are mildly injected. Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye and the corneas are clear on fluorescein staining.

data_table.Examination: Persistent central facial erythema with telangiectasia, papules and pustules across cheeks, nose and chin, no comedones
data_table.Ocular: Thickened erythematous lid margins with crusting at the lash bases, mild conjunctival injection
data_table.Ocular assessment: Visual acuity 6/6 each eye, corneas clear on fluorescein staining, no photophobia or eye pain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence topical benzoyl peroxide with adapalene applied each evening to the affected areas
options.rationale: This combination treats acne vulgaris, the near pair, which is distinguished by comedones, involvement of the back and chest, and a younger age of onset. Both agents are irritant on rosacea skin and typically worsen the erythema. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Cease the topical corticosteroid and commence an oral tetracycline with lid hygiene measures
options.rationale: Papulopustular rosacea with blepharitis is ocular rosacea, and an oral tetracycline treats both the cutaneous and the ocular disease where topical therapy treats only the skin. Withdrawing the corticosteroid is essential because it drives a steroid induced rosacea like eruption and causes rebound on cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Cease the topical corticosteroid and commence topical metronidazole gel applied twice daily
options.rationale: Topical metronidazole or ivermectin is appropriate first line treatment for mild to moderate papulopustular rosacea confined to the skin, and stopping the steroid is right. Topical therapy does not treat ocular involvement, which is what makes this case need systemic treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Continue the topical corticosteroid and add an oral antihistamine for the flushing episodes
options.rationale: Antihistamines target histamine mediated flushing such as that of mastocytosis or an allergic reaction, and they do not help rosacea. Continuing the corticosteroid perpetuates the atrophy and telangiectasia that are worsening her appearance. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment of the telangiectasia and background facial erythema
options.rationale: Vascular laser is genuinely effective for fixed erythema and telangiectasia and has a place once inflammation is controlled. It does nothing for papules, pustules or blepharitis, which are the active problems now. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory facial dermatosis of the central face, characterised by flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasia, and in the papulopustular subtype inflammatory papules and pustules without comedones. Ocular involvement occurs in around half of patients and can precede the skin disease, presenting as blepharitis with lid margin telangiectasia, meibomian gland dysfunction, a gritty foreign body sensation, recurrent chalazia and conjunctival injection. Oral tetracyclines are the treatment of choice when ocular disease is present, and their benefit is largely anti inflammatory rather than antibacterial, which is why subantimicrobial dosing also works. Topical corticosteroids must be stopped, since prolonged use produces a steroid induced rosacea like dermatitis with atrophy and rebound flaring. Trigger avoidance, daily sun protection and gentle non soap cleansing are part of every management plan, and persistent corneal involvement or visual symptoms require ophthalmology referral.
key_points: Absence of comedones separates rosacea from acne vulgaris.
Ocular rosacea affects around half of patients and can precede the skin disease.
Oral tetracyclines treat both cutaneous and ocular disease; topicals treat only the skin.
Topical corticosteroids cause a steroid induced rosacea and must be withdrawn.
Refer to ophthalmology for corneal involvement, photophobia or reduced acuity.
explanation.pearls: Doxycycline at 40 mg daily in a modified release form is as effective as 100 mg for rosacea while remaining below the antimicrobial threshold, which reduces both resistance pressure and the gastrointestinal and candidal adverse effects of full dose therapy.

subtopic_detail: recurrent hours long spinning with fluctuating low frequency hearing loss and ear fullness on one side
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 44-year-old woman with recurrent attacks of the room spinning. Over the past eight months she has had six episodes, each building over minutes, lasting three to four hours, and leaving her unsteady for a day afterwards. She vomits during them and has to lie still in a dark room.

She describes a sense of pressure and fullness in the left ear before and during each attack, with a low pitched roaring noise on that side, and says her hearing in that ear is muffled during an attack and improves between episodes. She has no headache with the attacks, no photophobia or visual aura, and no history of migraine. There is no positional trigger and the attacks come without warning. Between attacks her examination is normal with no nystagmus, normal gait and a negative head impulse test bilaterally. Weber lateralises to the right and Rinne is positive bilaterally. A pure tone audiogram taken last week shows a 35 decibel sensorineural loss at 250 and 500 Hz on the left with normal thresholds above 2000 Hz.

data_table.Attack pattern: Six episodes over eight months, each lasting three to four hours, with vomiting and no headache or visual aura
data_table.Otological: Left aural fullness and low pitched roaring tinnitus during attacks, fluctuating muffled hearing on the left
data_table.Examination: No spontaneous nystagmus between attacks, negative head impulse test bilaterally, Weber lateralises to the right, Rinne positive bilaterally
data_table.Audiometry: 35 decibel sensorineural loss at 250 and 500 Hz on the left with normal thresholds above 2000 Hz

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for intratympanic gentamicin injection to ablate vestibular function on the affected side
options.rationale: Chemical ablation is an effective option but is reserved for disabling attacks that persist despite medical therapy, because it carries a risk of further hearing loss. Offering it before any first line treatment has been tried is disproportionate. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Meniere disease)

options.text: Advise dietary salt restriction and commence betahistine with referral for otological review
options.rationale: Episodic vertigo lasting twenty minutes to twelve hours with documented low frequency sensorineural loss, aural fullness and roaring tinnitus is Meniere disease. Salt restriction with betahistine and specialist audiological follow up is the standard Australian first line approach. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence propranolol as migraine prophylaxis and provide a headache and vertigo diary
options.rationale: Vestibular migraine is the commonest cause of recurrent spontaneous vertigo and is the central near pair, so prophylaxis is a reasonable reflex. It requires a history of migraine and migrainous features with the attacks, and it does not produce a documented low frequency hearing loss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence a tapering course of oral prednisolone and refer for vestibular rehabilitation therapy
options.rationale: This is the treatment for vestibular neuritis, which causes a single prolonged attack over days with a positive head impulse test on the affected side and normal hearing. Recurrent discrete attacks with a normal head impulse test between them do not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Perform the Epley particle repositioning manoeuvre and teach her the Brandt Daroff exercises
options.rationale: Repositioning treats benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which gives seconds long positionally triggered spinning with a positive Dix Hallpike test and no auditory symptoms at all. Attacks lasting hours without a positional trigger are a different mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Meniere disease is thought to result from endolymphatic hydrops and is diagnosed on a clinical triad backed by audiometry: two or more spontaneous episodes of vertigo lasting twenty minutes to twelve hours, audiometrically documented low to mid frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the affected ear on at least one occasion, and fluctuating aural symptoms of hearing loss, tinnitus or fullness. The low frequency pattern of hearing loss is the feature that most reliably separates it from vestibular migraine, which is far commoner and produces episodic vertigo without any documented hearing loss but with migrainous features. Attack duration is the most useful single discriminator across the episodic vertigo syndromes: seconds for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, twenty minutes to twelve hours for Meniere disease, and days for vestibular neuritis. First line management is salt restriction with attention to caffeine and alcohol, betahistine, and a diuretic in some protocols, with vestibular sedatives used only for acute attacks because they impair central compensation. Escalation for refractory disabling disease includes intratympanic corticosteroid, intratympanic gentamicin and surgical procedures, and progressive hearing loss is managed with amplification.
key_points: Attack duration of twenty minutes to twelve hours is the Meniere window.
Low to mid frequency sensorineural loss on audiometry is required for the diagnosis.
Vestibular migraine is commoner, needs migrainous features, and spares the audiogram.
Vestibular sedatives are for acute attacks only, as they impede central compensation.
Ablative treatment is reserved for disabling disease refractory to medical therapy.
explanation.pearls: The low frequency pattern of hearing loss is what makes Meniere disease unusual, because almost every other cause of sensorineural loss, including presbyacusis, noise exposure and acoustic neuroma, takes the high frequencies first.

subtopic_detail: daily itchy weals for five months resolving within a day each and no response to a standard antihistamine dose
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman with itchy raised weals that have appeared almost every day for five months. Individual weals come up on the trunk and limbs, are intensely itchy, and fade completely within about twelve hours leaving no mark behind.

She has been taking cetirizine 10 mg once daily for three months with only partial benefit and is losing sleep. She has identified no food, drug or physical trigger, and the weals appear at rest as often as with exercise. She has had no lip, tongue or throat swelling, no abdominal pain and no breathing difficulty. She takes no other medications including no non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs. On examination there are scattered pink weals of varying size on the trunk and thighs, each blanching on pressure, with no purpura, no residual pigmentation and no scaling. There is no wheeze, the joints are not swollen, and she is afebrile with no weight loss. Full blood examination, C reactive protein and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Scattered blanching pink weals of varying size on trunk and thighs, no purpura, no residual pigmentation, no angioedema
data_table.Symptom pattern: Daily weals for five months, each individual lesion resolving within twelve hours without bruising
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination, C reactive protein and thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Current treatment: Cetirizine 10 mg once daily for three months with partial benefit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence a maintenance course of oral prednisolone with review of the dose every month
options.rationale: Short corticosteroid courses are occasionally used for severe exacerbations lasting a few days, so steroids are not entirely absent from the algorithm. Maintenance corticosteroid for a condition lasting years produces predictable and serious harm and is explicitly discouraged. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Increase the cetirizine dose up to fourfold the standard dose and review her response
options.rationale: Chronic spontaneous urticaria is treated with a second generation antihistamine, and updosing to up to four times the standard dose before escalating further is the established next step. Around half of patients who fail the standard dose respond to updosing, which is far safer than the alternatives. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Refer for omalizumab therapy after documenting her failure of standard antihistamine treatment
options.rationale: Omalizumab is highly effective and is the correct escalation, but Australian access requires documented failure of antihistamine at up to four times the standard dose. Referring before updosing means the step she most likely needs has not been tried. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Arrange a punch biopsy of a fresh lesion to look for a leucocytoclastic vasculitic pattern
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated for urticarial vasculitis, the near pair, which is suggested by individual weals lasting more than 24 hours, painful or burning rather than itchy lesions, and residual bruising or pigmentation. Her weals clear within twelve hours leaving normal skin. (Source: ASCIA: Chronic urticaria)

options.text: Arrange specific immunoglobulin E allergy testing to a panel of common foods and aeroallergens
options.rationale: Allergen testing is useful when the history points to a specific reproducible trigger with lesions appearing within an hour of exposure. Daily spontaneous weals over months are not allergic, and indiscriminate panel testing generates false positives that lead to unnecessary dietary restriction. (Source: ASCIA: Chronic urticaria)

explanation.summary: Chronic spontaneous urticaria is defined by weals, angioedema or both occurring for six weeks or longer without a consistent external trigger, and it affects around one per cent of the population with a strong female predominance. Most cases are autoimmune, mediated by immunoglobulin G autoantibodies against the high affinity immunoglobulin E receptor or against immunoglobulin E itself, and extensive allergy testing is therefore unhelpful and often misleading. The essential clinical discriminator is the life of an individual weal: a lesion that lasts under 24 hours and resolves without a mark is urticaria, while one that persists beyond 24 hours, burns rather than itches, or leaves bruising or pigmentation should be biopsied for urticarial vasculitis. The treatment ladder is a second generation antihistamine at standard dose, updosing to up to four times standard, then omalizumab, then ciclosporin, and maintenance oral corticosteroid has no place at any rung. Most cases remit spontaneously, around half within a year, which is a genuinely useful thing to tell a distressed patient.
key_points: Six weeks or more of weals without a consistent trigger defines the chronic spontaneous form.
Individual weals lasting under 24 hours without residual marks distinguish it from vasculitis.
Allergy testing is unhelpful because most cases are autoimmune rather than allergic.
Updose the second generation antihistamine to up to four times standard before escalating.
Maintenance oral corticosteroid is not part of the treatment ladder.
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient to circle a single weal with a pen and check it the next day, because a lesion still present at 24 hours or leaving pigmentation within the circle is the finding that turns an antihistamine prescription into a skin biopsy for urticarial vasculitis.
